title: Things to do in Assisi: 5 historic places to visit
description: Explore five Assisi places: San Francesco, Santa Chiara, San Rufino, Piazza del Comune and Rocca Maggiore, with entry advice, transport and a walking route.
relatedQueries: how to reach Assisi by train
intro: For a first visit to Assisi, concentrate on five places in the historic centre: the Basilica of San Francesco, Santa Chiara, the Cathedral of San Rufino, Piazza del Comune and Rocca Maggiore. Together they introduce the city through its religious and artistic heritage, the Roman and medieval layers of its public spaces, and the fortress that explains its position in the landscape. You can link the five on foot, but the centre has changes in level. Arrange your visits around your arrival point, opening arrangements and mobility rather than treating the map as a flat walking circuit.

Assisi is in Umbria, on the slopes of Mount Asio at the foot of Mount Subasio. The town and Franciscan sites have belonged to the World Heritage List since 2000. That property covers a much wider area than this selection: here the focus is the historic core, without adding transfers to outlying sanctuaries. One day can work if you choose how deeply to explore each interior. Staying overnight gives you more flexibility to divide the longer visits, rests and climb towards the fortress.

sections.heading: 1. Basilica of San Francesco: two churches within one visit
paragraphs: Give San Francesco enough time to distinguish its different spaces. The complex brings together an upper and a lower church, one above the other, and the crypt containing the saint’s tomb. Work on the lower church began in 1228 to house his remains. On approaching, notice how the square and its portico prepare the entrance, then compare the atmosphere below with the nave and stained glass above. These are different experiences within a single monumental complex, rather than two separate attractions added to make the list longer.

The art is more rewarding when you look beyond finding one famous picture. Painted cycles interact with chapels, transepts and the architecture itself. UNESCO highlights the role of works associated with Cimabue, Giotto, Simone Martini and Pietro Lorenzetti in European art history. An audioguide or an interpreted visit can help you understand what you are looking at. Choose that service for its content and availability, distinguishing it from ordinary admission. Leave room both for quiet observation and for people who have come principally to pray.

The Sacro Convento’s current information states that individual visitors enter free of charge without a compulsory ticket, while organised groups need a reservation. The operator publishes separate hours for the churches and tomb, including seasonal variations, services and an earlier Wednesday closing for the lower church. Check that specific calendar when planning your day. General opening should not be taken to mean that every space is available for sightseeing during every service. Avoid leaving the whole complex until a hurried final stop if you want to appreciate its different areas.

sections.heading: 2. Santa Chiara: pink stone, buttresses and an open square
paragraphs: Santa Chiara offers another perspective on the religious city. Its facade combines the characteristic white and pink stone of Mount Subasio, a central rose window and proportions worth examining from the side as well as straight ahead. The large reinforcing arches become apparent from that angle. Construction began in 1257 on the site of the earlier Church of San Giorgio. The broad square gives you room to step back, understand the building’s shape and appreciate its relationship with the view across the valley.

Inside, distinguish sightseeing areas from spaces dedicated to devotion. The chapel holds the crucifix brought from San Damiano; the account that it spoke to Francis belongs to religious tradition. Clare’s remains are in the crypt, while other elements of the church explain her memory and the community of Poor Clares. You can approach the building through spiritual or historical interests, following the site’s instructions and giving worshippers room. The visit becomes more meaningful when it extends beyond a photograph in front of the facade.

The basilica is close to Porta Nuova and makes a useful end or starting point for a walk through the centre. For motorists, municipal information identifies the Porta Nuova car park as the reference point for Santa Chiara. Treat the square and the interior as different planning decisions: the former can provide a pause in the walk, while the latter depends on opening and religious activity. If a particular area, such as the crypt, is central to your plans, confirm its arrangements rather than inferring them from access to the square.

sections.heading: 3. San Rufino Cathedral: read the facade, then change periods
paragraphs: The climb along Via San Rufino from Piazza del Comune leads to the city’s cathedral. It is particularly interesting for comparing architecture. Alongside the Franciscan basilicas, this Romanesque facade offers portals, rose windows and decoration featuring plants, animals and human figures. Stop to examine those details before entering. Comparing the central rose window with the smaller lateral ones helps you read a facade that can otherwise appear densely decorated when seen only in passing.

The interior tells a later chapter. During the sixteenth century, Galeazzo Alessi worked on the complex and transformed its spaces using Renaissance forms. The contrast between outside and inside illustrates how a monument can belong to several periods rather than one frozen moment. The tourism information also associates the baptismal font with Francis and Clare, presenting that connection as tradition or legend. Preserve that distinction when reading the building. Its interest does not depend on treating every devotional account as an independently demonstrated historical fact.

San Rufino is in the upper part of the centre near Piazza Matteotti and can be paired with the approach towards Rocca Maggiore. Before adding the diocesan museum, crypt or other lower spaces, check their own opening and entry conditions. Entering a church does not automatically provide admission to all its cultural areas. If you prefer a less demanding walk, pause here before deciding on the remaining climb. Being close on a map does not remove the slopes or steps involved in a particular route.

sections.heading: 4. Piazza del Comune: Roman and medieval Assisi in one space
paragraphs: Piazza del Comune shifts the focus from large religious buildings to urban public life. The Temple of Minerva, civic palaces, Torre del Popolo and fountain of the three lions bring different periods and purposes around the same square. Use it as an orientation point between the basilicas and San Rufino. Look at the ensemble first, then pick out details: the rhythm of the ancient columns, the forms of the medieval buildings and the ways in which streets enter this open space.

The building known as the Temple of Minerva preserves a facade of six Corinthian columns dating to the second half of the first century BC. Behind it stands the Church of Santa Maria sopra Minerva, shaped by later transformations, including sixteenth-century work and Baroque alterations. The classical frontage therefore does not lead into an untouched Roman interior; comparing the two is part of its appeal. The tourism entry identifies accessibility limitations. Ask about the specific entrance if you need to avoid steps, rather than assuming a traversable square means easy entry into every building.

For this selection, the square and temple count as one stop. Take the opportunity to rest or adjust your schedule without automatically adding every nearby museum to an already full day. The Roman Forum is an archaeological route with its own entry and ticket; looking at the temple facade is not the same as visiting it. Check the municipal options if you want to explore that layer further. Via San Rufino leads uphill from the square towards the cathedral.

sections.heading: 5. Rocca Maggiore: the fortress and the town from above
paragraphs: Rocca Maggiore stands at the summit of Mount Asio and helps explain Assisi’s relationship with the valley. Walls, towers and later additions show a defensive purpose different from that of the churches below. The present structure includes fourteenth-century rebuilding associated with Cardinal Albornoz and work from subsequent periods. Its viewpoints connect the town, slopes and surrounding landscape. Visibility depends on conditions, so it is better to value the architecture and setting rather than make a guaranteed sunset the fixed point of your entire visit.

Exploring the building is also part of the experience. Italy’s Ministry of Culture describes levels of the main keep connected by a spiral staircase, alongside walls and towers added during its evolution. This matters for visitors with reduced mobility, small children or a preference for avoiding narrow sections. Ask which specific parts of the route are suitable and accessible. Reaching the entrance is a different question from visiting every interior and elevated viewpoint. Choose the extent of the visit around your circumstances instead of treating every climb as compulsory.

The municipal page updated in October 2026 lists ordinary admission at €8, with November to February hours of 10:00 to 17:00 and a December 25 closure. Confirm the information for your date and leave a margin before closing. The €10 combined option covers Rocca Maggiore, the Roman Forum and civic Pinacoteca with an audioguide. It is relevant if you want those three museums, rather than automatically being necessary for the five places in this guide. From the San Rufino area, a walking approach can be arranged through the Porta Perlici sector.

sections.heading: Reaching the centre and choosing where to start
paragraphs: When planning a railway journey, distinguish Assisi station from the historic centre. Trenitalia offers Assisi Link, combining the train with a bus departing from the forecourt outside the station. Use Assisi Centro as the origin or destination when searching for the combined journey. The tourism office identifies this connection as line C. Check the actual timetable, current service notices and the stop that suits your arrival plans; stepping off a train should not be treated as arriving directly in front of one of the basilicas.

If you are driving, the centre has a restricted traffic zone requiring the appropriate authorisation. A practical alternative is to choose an outside car park that fits the beginning of your walk: Giovanni Paolo II for the San Francesco side, Porta Nuova for Santa Chiara or Piazza Matteotti for the upper town. If staying inside the centre, ask your accommodation about the actual access arrangements. Sorting out that first transfer can prevent an unnecessary uphill start with luggage.

sections.heading: Bookings, scope and adapting the route to your visit
paragraphs: Separate three decisions: an individual or group visit to San Francesco, entry to the fortress and any additional museums. The municipal combined ticket does not replace the reservation for a group at the basilica. Equally, an audioguide or optional experience does not become compulsory admission simply because it appears on a booking portal. Choose the products that fit what you actually want to see and read their official conditions. This makes it easier to anticipate spending without adding services you do not need.

For walking, prioritise comfortable footwear, breaks and an order that avoids repeatedly climbing the same slopes. Rain may encourage longer interior visits, subject to opening; in reduced visibility, the fortress still has architectural interest even if the panorama is limited. If you need a route without steps, request specific information before choosing it. Broad accessibility labels do not describe every street, chapel, tower or staircase. You can shorten this proposal around your needs without making the visit any less worthwhile.

itinerary: Starting from San Francesco, spend the first part of the visit distinguishing the churches and crypt where sightseeing is allowed. Continue towards Piazza del Comune, taking a break and examining the Temple of Minerva facade. Decide on the San Rufino and Rocca Maggiore block according to the fortress timetable and your willingness to climb. Leave a realistic space for food, and consult religious services before fixing a rigid sequence of interiors.

Finish with Santa Chiara and its square when its hours allow, or move that block to the beginning if arriving through Porta Nuova. With an overnight stay, separate the upper town and longer visits from the walk between the two basilicas. This is an organisational suggestion, not a timed itinerary: the time spent looking, queues, mobility and your return transport determine how much is sensible to include.

faq.question: Is one day enough for these five Assisi places?
faq.answer: It can work for selected visits across the five, provided you coordinate opening arrangements and choose how deeply to explore each interior. The fortress climb and time spent on the art make a substantial difference to pacing. An overnight stay makes it easier to divide the route and take breaks without relying on one return connection.

faq.question: Do individual visitors need to buy a San Francesco entry ticket?
faq.answer: The Sacro Convento’s own booking portal states that individual admission is free and does not require a ticket. Groups need to reserve. Guided visits, audioguides and other services have separate conditions, so identify the particular product before treating its price as the ordinary admission charge.

faq.question: Is Assisi railway station inside the historic centre?
faq.answer: Rail travel is followed by a transfer to the centre. Assisi Link provides a bus from the station forecourt, with the combined journey searched as Assisi Centro. Check the timetable and the stop appropriate for your chosen starting point, together with the connection back.

faq.question: Does the combined ticket include every basilica?
faq.answer: The municipal combined ticket consulted covers Rocca Maggiore, the Roman Forum and civic Pinacoteca, with an audioguide. It is not a universal pass for every building in the town and does not replace arrangements for an organised religious group. Decide whether you want all three museums before selecting it.

faq.question: Can the whole walk be done without slopes or stairs?
faq.answer: Assisi is built on a hill and several sections in this proposal ascend. The fortress adds interior staircases, while the Temple of Minerva has entry limitations. Ask the tourism office and each site about a route appropriate to your requirements; a short distance alone does not establish complete accessibility.

conclusion: Assisi is more rewarding when its places are connected: the Franciscan basilicas, cathedral, civic square and fortress show different functions within a town that looks small on a map but offers rich routes. Choose visits around your interests and the time available. For a wider cultural journey through Italy, the related Perugia, Siena and Ferrara guides provide other perspectives without repeating this first introduction.
